strategies.title: The 4 Ds
strategies.summary: Delay, deep breaths, drink water, do something else
strategies.body: Most urges pass within 3 to 5 minutes. These 4 steps help you get through one.
steps: Delay. Give it 5 minutes before you decide anything.
Deep breaths. Take 20 slow ones.
Drink water. Sip a cold glass slowly.
Do something else. Step outside, call someone or climb the stairs.

sources.title: Cravings and withdrawal when you stop smoking
I can't survive without my first smoke or vape

strategies.title: Delay
strategies.summary: Wait 5 to 10 minutes while the urge peaks and passes
strategies.body: An urge rises, peaks and fades, usually within a few minutes. Start the timer and leave the decision until it ends.
steps: Choose 5 to 10 minutes and start the timer.
Keep your hands busy while it runs.
When it ends, check how strong the urge is now.
If it's still there, give it another 5 minutes.

sources.title: I can't survive without my first smoke or vape

strategies.title: Ride out the urge
strategies.summary: Let it rise and fade without acting on it
strategies.body: Treat an urge like a wave: don't fight it and don't act on it. Most fade within a few minutes, and they get weaker over time.
steps: Notice the urge and say what you feel, like “I want a dose and my chest feels tight.”
Stay with the feeling without doing anything about it.
Remind yourself it will pass.

strategies.title: Answer the urge back
strategies.summary: Spot the thought behind it and answer it
strategies.body: Urges come with thoughts like “I deserve one” or “one more won't matter”. Once you've spotted them, they're easier to answer.
steps: Notice the thought that comes just before or during an urge.
Answer it with your own reason for cutting down.
If it's stress talking, take a break to breathe instead.
Write down 2 thoughts that catch you out, with an answer for each.

strategies.title: Write down your reasons
strategies.summary: Why you're coming off NRT, in your own words
strategies.body: When an urge comes, it helps to see, in your own words, why you're coming off NRT.
steps: Write 3 reasons you want to stop using NRT.
Keep them where you'll see them, like your lock screen or the fridge.
Read them when an urge starts.

strategies.title: After a slip
strategies.summary: A one-off doesn't undo what you've done
strategies.body: Going over the guide, or smoking or vaping again, doesn't undo what you've done. It shows you where the hard moments are.
steps: Treat a one-off as a one-off and carry on with the plan.
Think about what set it off: stress, other people or a feeling.
Write down how you'll handle it next time, and keep the note where you'll see it.
If you're smoking or vaping regularly again, a stop smoking service can help you set a new quit date.

sources.title: Getting back on track after a smoking relapse

strategies.title: Talk to a quit coach
strategies.summary: Free advice from people who know NRT well
strategies.body: Stop smoking services and quitlines are free. Their advisers know NRT well and can help with urges, triggers and how you use your products.
steps: Call your local quitline or stop smoking service.
Say you've stopped smoking or vaping and you're cutting down NRT.
Ask about the pace of your plan, and what helps on hard days.

sources.title: NHS stop smoking services help you quit
Six quick tips for using quit smoking medicines

strategies.title: Deep breaths
strategies.summary: Box breathing or 4-7-8, for 1 to 3 minutes
strategies.body: Slow, counted breathing can calm you when stress pushes you towards a dose. Follow the timer for 1 to 3 minutes.
steps: Sit or stand with your feet flat on the floor and your shoulders loose.
Box breathing: in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4.
4-7-8 breathing: in through your nose for 4, hold for 7, out through your mouth for 8.
If 4-7-8 feels too long, use box breathing instead.

sources.publisher: Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Trust
sources.title: Breathing techniques

strategies.title: Move for 5 minutes
strategies.summary: A brisk walk or the stairs while it passes
strategies.body: A quick burst of activity uses up restless energy and gives an urge time to pass.
steps: Walk briskly, outside if you can.
If you can't get out, climb the stairs or do 10 squats.
Notice how strong the urge is when you stop.

strategies.title: Relax your muscles one by one
strategies.summary: Tense and let go, one part at a time
strategies.body: Tensing and then letting go of each part of your body in turn eases tension. It also helps you notice when you're tensing up.
steps: Lie down or sit somewhere comfortable.
Breathe in and tense one area, like your right hand and arm, for a few seconds.
Breathe out and let it go.
Work through your arms, legs, stomach, chest, back, shoulders, neck and face. Skip any part that hurts.

strategies.title: Look after yourself when you're low
strategies.summary: Move, plan your day and talk to someone
strategies.body: Mood can dip for a while as your body adjusts. A dose may seem to help, but it only eases withdrawal for a while.
steps: Get outside and move, even for a few minutes.
Plan your day, with something you enjoy in it.
Talk to someone you trust every day.
If you don't feel better in 2 weeks, or it feels like too much, talk to a GP.
If you feel you might harm yourself, call your local emergency number now.

sources.title: Stopping smoking for your mental health

strategies.title: Pick another treat
strategies.summary: Mark a good moment with something else
strategies.body: If a dose is how you mark a good moment, find something else that feels like a reward.
steps: Make a short list of small treats: a favourite snack, a song, a film or time outside.
When you'd usually celebrate with a dose, have one of those instead.

strategies.title: Tie treats to milestones
strategies.summary: Spend what you save on something you enjoy
strategies.body: Cutting down is worth marking. Spending what you save on NRT gives each week something to show for it.
steps: Work out what a week of NRT costs you.
Each week you cut down, spend some of the difference on a small treat.
Save the rest for something bigger when the plan ends.

strategies.title: Make each dose a decision
strategies.summary: Rate the urge before each dose
strategies.body: On autopilot, a dose can happen before you've noticed. A short pause turns it back into a choice.
steps: Keep your NRT in one place, not in every pocket and bag.
Before each dose, rate the urge from 1 to 5.
If it's a 1 or 2, wait 5 minutes first.
Add a tag when you log it, so you can see the pattern later.

strategies.title: Give your hands something to do
strategies.summary: Something to hold where you'd reach for NRT
strategies.body: Holding something breaks the habit of reaching for NRT, especially on calls, in front of a screen or when you're bored.
steps: Keep a squeeze ball, a pen to doodle with or a fidget toy where you'd usually reach for NRT.
Try a few now, before you need them, to find one that works.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Keep a list of distractions
strategies.summary: Quick things to do, written down in advance
strategies.body: Urges fade faster when your mind is busy. A list made in advance means you don't have to think of something in the moment.
steps: Write down 5 quick things you enjoy, like a song, a puzzle, a call or a funny video.
Try each one this week to see what works.
Keep the list on your phone and pick one as soon as an urge starts.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Change rooms
strategies.summary: Go somewhere else until it passes
strategies.body: Urges are tied to places and routines. Moving, even to another room, breaks the pattern long enough for an urge to pass.
steps: Get up and go somewhere else, or step outside for fresh air.
Do something there that needs your hands.
Come back once the urge has faded.

sources.title: Cravings and withdrawal when you stop smoking

strategies.title: Move the dose to before the meal
strategies.summary: Have it before you eat, not after
strategies.body: If a dose follows every meal, the meal becomes the cue. Having that dose before you eat breaks the link without adding one.
steps: Have your usual after-meal dose before the meal instead.
Time it so it's finished before you start eating. Gum and lozenges work less well with food and drink.
When the meal ends, get up from the table.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Get up from the table
strategies.summary: Leave as soon as you finish eating
strategies.body: The end of a meal, or of a coffee or tea, is a common cue. Doing something different straight away breaks it.
steps: Get up as soon as you've finished.
Brush your teeth or chew ordinary sugar-free gum.
Clear the table, wash up or go for a short walk.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Time drinks around gum and lozenges
strategies.summary: Coffee and fizzy drinks stop gum and lozenges working as well
strategies.body: Coffee, fizzy drinks and other acidic food and drink can stop gum and lozenges working as well, so each one does less for the urge.
steps: Don't eat or drink for 15 minutes before a piece of gum or a lozenge.
Don't eat or drink while it's in your mouth.

strategies.title: Swap the drink for a while
strategies.summary: Juice or hot water with lemon, somewhere new
strategies.body: If coffee or tea and a dose go together, the drink becomes the cue. Swapping it for a few weeks loosens the link.
steps: Try juice, or hot water with lemon.
Have it somewhere different from usual.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings
I can't survive without my first smoke or vape

strategies.title: Keep your mouth busy
strategies.summary: Mints, sugar-free gum or something to chew
strategies.body: When you can't get up and leave, like when you're driving or at a table, something to chew or sip helps.
steps: Carry sugar-free mints or ordinary sugar-free gum.
Try a toothpick, a straw or a cinnamon stick.
Snack on carrot or celery sticks.

strategies.title: Start the day with something else
strategies.summary: Start the day with something that isn't nicotine
strategies.body: The first dose of the day is often the hardest to move. Putting something else first makes the morning less about NRT.
steps: Have a glass of water, a shower or breakfast before anything else.
Then check how strong the urge is.
Each week, try to have the first dose a little later.

sources.title: I can't survive without my first smoke or vape

strategies.title: Wind down without a dose
strategies.summary: A calmer last hour before bed
strategies.body: A dose late in the evening can become part of going to bed, and nicotine can affect sleep. A calmer last hour makes it easier to go without.
steps: Skip caffeine from late afternoon.
Put your phone away once you're in bed.
Read or have a bath to relax.
Keep the same bedtime and wake-up time, even at weekends.

sources.title: Cravings and withdrawal when you stop smoking

strategies.title: Change the commute
strategies.summary: A new route, new music or something to chew
strategies.body: Driving, walking the same way and waiting for transport are common cues. A small change to the routine weakens them.
steps: Take a different route for a while.
Put on new music or a podcast.
Keep something to chew or hold in the car or your bag.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Change your breaks
strategies.summary: A different time, place or company
strategies.body: If a break usually means a dose, the break itself becomes the cue.
steps: Take your break at a different time.
Spend it walking, or with colleagues who don't smoke or vape.
Have water or a snack instead.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Cool down with water first
strategies.summary: Water and a stretch after a workout
strategies.body: If a dose usually follows a workout, fill those minutes with water and a stretch instead.
steps: Drink a full glass of water straight after.
Stretch for about 5 minutes to cool down.
Then check whether the urge is still there.

sources.title: Cravings and withdrawal when you stop smoking

strategies.title: Decide your limit before you go out
strategies.summary: Decide how many doses fit tonight before you go
strategies.body: Drinking and nights out are common cues. Deciding before you go takes the choice out of the moment.
steps: Before you go, decide how many doses fit tonight.
Log each one as you go, so you can keep count.
Have a soft drink between alcoholic ones, or go alcohol-free.
Have a line ready in case someone offers you a cigarette or vape.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Have a line ready
strategies.summary: Know what you'll say if someone offers
strategies.body: Being around people who smoke or vape, or being offered one, is easier when you've already decided what to say.
steps: Pick a short line, like “No thanks, I've stopped.”
Ask friends who smoke or vape not to offer, and not to do it right next to you.
For the first few weeks, meet them somewhere smoking isn't allowed.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings

strategies.title: Tell someone you're cutting down
strategies.summary: Someone to message when an urge is strong
strategies.body: People who know what you're doing can help in the moment. A call or a message is often enough to get past an urge.
steps: Tell a friend or someone at home about your plan.
Ask if you can message them when an urge is strong.
Let them know you might be short-tempered for a while, and ask for patience.

sources.title: Understand your smoking triggers and cravings
Cravings and withdrawal when you stop smoking

strategies.title: Remember withdrawal passes
strategies.summary: It's strongest in the first week, then fades
strategies.body: Withdrawal is uncomfortable, but it can't hurt you. It's usually strongest in the first week and fades over 3 to 4 weeks. Cutting down can bring some of it back for a while.
steps: Remind yourself the feeling is temporary.
Use the 4 Ds when an urge hits.
Give yourself credit for each one you get through.

strategies.title: Ask about slowing the plan
strategies.summary: A pharmacist or GP can help you go slower
strategies.body: Using NRT for longer is far safer than going back to smoking. If withdrawal is strong or keeps coming back, a pharmacist or GP can help you set a slower pace.
steps: Note when the urges are worst and how strong they get.
Show a pharmacist or GP your last few weeks in the app.
Ask whether a slower taper would suit you.

sources.title: Find the best stop-smoking products for you
Quit smoking with nicotine replacement therapies (NRTs)

strategies.title: Use each dose the way the pack says
strategies.summary: How gum and lozenges work best
strategies.body: Nicotine gum and lozenges work differently from ordinary gum and sweets. Used properly, each one does more for the urge.
steps: Gum: bite slowly until it tingles, then park it between your cheek and gum for about a minute. Repeat until the tingling stops, usually about 30 minutes.
Lozenge: let it dissolve slowly between your cheek and gum. Don't chew or swallow it.
Sprays, inhalators and other forms: follow the leaflet in your pack.

sources.title: Six quick tips for using quit smoking medicines

strategies.title: Check if it's hunger
strategies.summary: Eat first, then see if the urge is still there
strategies.body: Hunger and an urge for nicotine can feel alike, so it's easy to mistake one for the other.
steps: Eat 3 meals a day, with a snack every 3 to 4 hours if you need one.
Keep fruit, carrot sticks or celery to hand.
If it's been a while since you ate, eat first and see if the urge is still there.

sources.title: Cravings and withdrawal when you stop smoking

strategies.title: Go easy on a foggy day
strategies.summary: Water, food and a short walk
strategies.body: Feeling tired or foggy is common while your body adjusts to less nicotine, and it usually passes.
steps: Drink a glass of water, and eat if it's been 3 to 4 hours.
Walk for a few minutes, outside if you can.
Save the hardest tasks for when you feel sharpest.
If you're tired all the time and rest doesn't help, see a GP.
